source.title_on_document: Exploring the impact of ChatGPT on college students’ mathematical creativity: A quasi-experimental study

supplement.holds: No supplementary material or appendix is identified in the supplied document. Table 5 and the main Results text contain the creativity statistics (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 49-50).

paper_design_summary: College students volunteering at Yangzhou University were assigned to solve open-ended mathematical creativity tasks with ChatGPT and structured prompting guidance or with traditional tools and no assistance; the Methods explicitly states random assignment in a supervised classroom, despite the quasi-experimental label in the title (PDF pp. 1, 4-7; printed pp. 39, 42-45). The analyzed sample comprised 124 students: 60 in the ChatGPT group and 64 in the control group (PDF p. 5, Figure 1, and p. 7, Participants/Table 2; printed pp. 43, 45). Two scorers classified and scored the participants’ solutions for flexibility, fluency and originality, with each indicator summed across four tasks produced while the assigned assistance was available; the post-task questionnaire measured self-evaluation and perceptions (PDF pp. 8-11, printed pp. 46-49).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students were assigned to task resolution with ChatGPT or task resolution without ChatGPT. Procedure explicitly reports random assignment, but does not describe sequence generation or allocation concealment. The title and abstract call the study quasi-experimental; classification follows the explicit allocation statement.
assignment.quote: All students were randomly assigned to either the experimental group (task resolution with ChatGPT) or the control group (task resolution without ChatGPT).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 42), Methods, Procedure; conflicting label on PDF p. 1 (printed p. 39), title and abstract.

arms.name: Experimental (task resolution with ChatGPT)
arms.description: Students used ChatGPT on personal computers, with introductory guidance and structured prompts for generating, checking and refining solutions (PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 43-45, Procedure, Figure 2 and Table 1). Analyzed group size is shown in Figure 1 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43).

arms.name: Control (task resolution without ChatGPT)
arms.description: Students solved the same tasks using traditional tools, such as paper and pencil, without support or external prompts (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Figure 1 and Procedure). Analyzed group size is shown in Figure 1.

participants.exclusions: Students who withdrew were not included in the analysis and their questionnaires were not collected; none of the collected questionnaires were excluded. Initial assignment totals and withdrawal counts by arm are not reported. Figure 1 does not distinguish initial allocation from retained participants, so randomized counts remain null. The reported sample and arm sizes are coded as analyzed (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure; PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Figure 1; PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Participants/Table 2).
participants.who: College students at Yangzhou University recruited across majors by counsellors, volunteering for course credits. The authors report no specific mathematics background and similar prior mathematics-course performance. Sessions were supervised in a quiet classroom, with participants working in separate areas (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure; PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Participants).
participants.quote: Since no prior sample size calculation was performed, a sensitivity analysis was conducted based on the sample size (n = 124)
participants.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 45), Participants and Table 2; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43), Figure 1, for N = 60 and N = 64; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 42), Procedure, for recruitment, country and withdrawals.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT; GPT-4o is shown by the model label in Figure 2 (PDF p. 6, printed p. 44). Exact model snapshot is not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Students interacted with ChatGPT through a browser, entered prompts, received solutions and feedback, and could request modifications or upload documents. The experimental group received technical training and structured example, heuristic, task-reminder, critical-thinking and divergent-thinking prompts. Interaction logs were recorded and students could not switch models. This is interactive chat with prompting support; the examples include supplied solution ideas (PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 43-45, Procedure, Figures 1-2 and Table 1).

task.description: Four open-ended mathematical creativity tasks: draw distinct 2 cm² figures in a 4 × 4 grid; devise methods to measure dispersion of five marbles; identify properties of the size and shape of water in a tilted rectangular prism; and, among eight geometries, identify shapes sharing features with shape A and describe those features. A separate number-pyramid creativity task measured baseline performance before the intervention (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Measures/Table 3/MCT; PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Figure 1).
task.duration: The experiment lasted 72 minutes (SD = 7) in the experimental group and 60 minutes (SD = 5) in the control group. These are the reported experiment durations, not a stated common time limit (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Procedure).

outcomes.name: MCT flexibility
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct correct answer categories within a participant’s solutions. This measures within-person flexibility. Two scorers independently marked solutions as correct or incorrect and classified the correct solutions; discrepancies were resolved to agreement. Each indicator was summed across the four tasks for each participant. Scorer qualifications and blinding are not stated (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring). The independent-sample t test and ANCOVA adjusting for prior ChatGPT experience analyze the same outcome (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Data analysis; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 49-50, Results).

contrasts.reported: Experimental M = 15.12, SD = 3.71; Control M = 12.50, SD = 3.49; t(122) = 4.05, d = 0.73, p = 0.000 (as printed in Table 5). Analyzed arm sizes: Experimental N = 60 and Control N = 64 (Figure 1). ANCOVA controlling for prior ChatGPT experience: F(1,121) = 16.60, η²p = 0.12, p < 0.001. The Table 5 note and Data analysis section state that p values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 49), Table 5 row 4 and Results, H1a-c; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43), Figure 1, for arm sizes; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 46), Data analysis. PDF p. 7 (printed p. 45), Participants/Table 2, confirms the analyzed sample.

outcomes.name: MCT originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Frequency-based rarity score derived from manually classified answer categories. The paper calculates each category’s proportion of total responses and assigns 3, 2 and 1 points to the printed bands "0, 1%; 1%, 2%; or 2%, 3%", respectively. For Task 1, category originality scores are summed within a participant, with each category counted once. The category-frequency reference pool and exact boundary conventions are not explicitly defined. Coded category_count because the score derives from category frequencies under a fixed scoring rule; the human scorers classify answers. Two scorers independently marked solutions as correct or incorrect and classified the correct solutions; discrepancies were resolved to agreement. Each indicator was summed across the four tasks for each participant. Scorer qualifications and blinding are not stated (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring). The independent-sample t test and ANCOVA adjusting for prior ChatGPT experience analyze the same outcome (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Data analysis; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 49-50, Results).

contrasts.reported: Experimental M = 4.82, SD = 2.64; Control M = 3.78, SD = 2.29; t(122) = 2.34, d = 0.42, p = 0.021. Analyzed arm sizes: Experimental N = 60 and Control N = 64 (Figure 1). ANCOVA controlling for prior ChatGPT experience: F(1,121) = 5.44, η²p = 0.04, p = 0.021. The Table 5 note and Data analysis section state that p values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Possible, unconfirmed overlap with c089: Liu et al. (2025), Who Is the Best Helper for University Students' Mathematical Creativity? (DOI 10.1002/cae.70100). Its Human-ChatGPT group and c471's Experimental group have the same analyzed size and identical reported age mean/SD, gender, major and prior ChatGPT experience counts. This cross-paper match suggests possible overlap but does not establish shared participants. Neither examined recruitment account identifies a shared sample; author confirmation is needed for shared-sample handling in pooled estimates.

eligibility.reason: All three criteria are met. Methods explicitly reports individual random assignment to task resolution with ChatGPT or without ChatGPT (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure); the supervised classroom setting supports lab_rct. Figure 1 reports the two analyzed groups as N = 60 and N = 64, and Participants reports n = 124 (PDF pp. 5 and 7, printed pp. 43 and 45, Figure 1/Participants/Table 2). Two scorers classified and scored students' actual solutions for flexibility, fluency and originality, summing each indicator across four tasks (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring); Table 5 reports the participant-level contrasts (PDF p. 11, printed p. 49). ChatGPT was available during production, so all three outcomes answer with_ai (PDF pp. 5-6, printed pp. 43-44, Procedure/Figures 1-2). The quasi-experimental title does not override the explicit allocation statement. Unreported randomization details, initial allocation/withdrawal counts and scoring details do not leave an eligibility criterion unresolved. Possible shared participants with c089 require clarification for pooling, not for these three criteria.

one_line_finding: Among 124 analyzed students, the ChatGPT group scored higher than controls on mathematical flexibility (d = 0.73), fluency (d = 0.66) and originality (d = 0.42) (PDF p. 11, printed p. 49, Table 5; sample size: PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Participants).
open_questions: The randomization mechanism and allocation concealment are not described, while the title/abstract use the conflicting quasi-experimental label (PDF pp. 1 and 4, printed pp. 39 and 42).
Initial randomized totals and withdrawals by arm are not reported (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 42-43, Procedure/Figure 1).
The originality-category reference pool and exact frequency-band boundaries are not explicitly defined (PDF p. 9, printed p. 47, Mathematical creativity scoring).
Scorer qualifications and blinding to condition are not stated (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring).

Possible participant overlap with c089, Liu et al. (2025), Who Is the Best Helper for University Students' Mathematical Creativity? (DOI 10.1002/cae.70100), remains unconfirmed. The two papers' ChatGPT groups have the same analyzed size and identical reported age mean/SD, gender, major and prior ChatGPT experience counts. This cross-paper match suggests possible overlap but does not establish shared participants; author confirmation would settle sample identity (c471 PDF pp. 4-5 and 7, printed pp. 42-43 and 45, Procedure/Figure 1/Table 2; c089 PDF pp. 3-4, Procedure/Participants/Table 1).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-09. Both raw forms parsed successfully. The entire markdown conversion was read in five contiguous chunks through the references and final citation; it contains no appendix or identified supplement. All retained numerical values were checked against the relevant PDF pages; Figures 1 and 2 were rendered and inspected in memory to verify arm counts and the model label. Locators use one-based PDF page positions and printed journal page numbers. No effect size, standard error or confidence interval was calculated. Outcomes were matched by name and construct, not array position: A lists originality, flexibility, fluency; B lists flexibility, fluency, originality. The only substantive disagreement is the originality measure code. The category-frequency scoring rule supports B’s category_count classification; manual coding of the categories does not make this a subjective novelty rating. Outcome order/IDs, synonymous arm names, prose, supplementary locator detail and unused synthesis placeholders were not counted as differences. The forms agree substantively on design, assignment, arms, counts, AI tool/role, task, outcome inventory, constructs/questions/units/availability/timing/primary status, numerical statistics, supplement status, sample overlap, company involvement, eligibility and finding. Their equivalent information was consolidated, including the adjustment statements that A placed in notes and B repeated with each contrast. Table 5 includes baseline creativity, self-efficacy, MCT flexibility/fluency/originality, self-evaluation, bias indices, interest, difficulty, effort and perceived ChatGPT usefulness (PDF p. 11, printed p. 49). Only the three MCT performance indicators are output-creativity outcomes produced during the assigned condition. Baseline creativity precedes the intervention; the self-reports and calibration bias indices do not assess the creativity/diversity of produced output. Figure 1’s post-test is a metacognitive questionnaire, not another unassisted creativity task. No after_ai or across_people outcome is reported. Rarity scores evaluate individual solutions, and flexibility is within-person variety. Neither is a between-person diversity contrast. No post-intervention overall-creativity composite or task-specific treatment contrasts are reported. The paper states hypotheses for the three indicators but does not designate a primary outcome or identify preregistration; primary remains not_stated. Table 5 p values and ANCOVA p values are reported as Benjamini-Hochberg corrected (PDF p. 11, printed p. 49, Table 5 note; PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Data analysis). The printed p = 0.000 entries and all d, F and partial eta-squared values are retained as printed. No numerical standard errors or confidence intervals are reported for these creativity contrasts. The intervention included structured prompts absent from the control, and the AI group spent longer on the experiment; the authors identify both as interpretation limits (PDF p. 14, printed p. 52, Discussion; PDF p. 17, printed p. 55, Limitations). External-resource instructions conflict: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43) allows browsing but reports that nobody did so; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 44) prohibits external resources. Both accounts describe ChatGPT as the aid used. No public data or code URL is identified. Unreported source details remain in open_questions; they do not constitute unresolved disagreements between the forms. Finalized on 2026-10-09 after independently reading the full markdown in five contiguous chunks through its final citation, checking the relevant PDF passages and all retained numerical statistics, and inspecting Figures 1 and 2 in memory. The assignment, outcome and people challenge files all contain empty problems arrays; therefore challenge_resolution is empty and all three challenge-disposition counts are zero. The current supplement field and analyzed-count wording already meet the form specification. The existing reconciliation object is unchanged and has no unresolved differences. The people checker's possible-overlap observation was independently confirmed at the level of matching reported group size and demographic distributions in the two local PDFs; sample identity remains unconfirmed and has been made explicit in sample_overlap and open_questions. All five open questions are classified in final.open_items; none prevents a decision on the three eligibility criteria.

open_items.item: Randomization mechanism and allocation concealment are not described, and the title/abstract use the quasi-experimental label. Author clarification would settle these reporting details; criterion 1 is met by the explicit statement that all students were randomly assigned, and the codebook does not require concealment details (PDF pp. 1 and 4, printed pp. 39 and 42).

Initial randomized totals and withdrawals by arm remain unreported. Author-provided allocation and attrition counts would settle this; criterion 2 is met by the documented 124 analyzed people, including 60 in the ChatGPT group and 64 controls (PDF pp. 4-5 and 7, printed pp. 42-43 and 45, Procedure/Figure 1/Participants/Table 2).

The originality-category reference pool and exact frequency-band boundaries remain unspecified. Authors could provide the complete scoring rule; this affects replication and interpretation of originality scores, while criterion 3 is already met by the documented scoring of produced solutions (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring).

Scorer qualifications and blinding to condition remain unreported. Authors could provide these details; they affect assessment of scoring bias, while criterion 3 requires output scoring rather than a particular scorer qualification or blinding procedure (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring).

Possible overlap with c089's Human-ChatGPT group remains unconfirmed despite identical reported group size and demographic distributions. Authors could confirm participant identity across the two papers; this affects shared-sample handling and pooling, not random assignment, the analyzed-person threshold or output scoring in c471 (c471 PDF pp. 4-5 and 7, printed pp. 42-43 and 45; c089 PDF pp. 3-4, Procedure/Participants/Table 1).
